## 2026-11-19: LLVM optimization becomes the standard bytecode pipeline

User clarification and authorization: optimize the guest Tower program through
LLVM, then translate optimized LLVM IR back to Tower bytecode. Compiling the
interpreter implementation with LLVM is not the requested optimization. Make
`Tower graph -> LLVM IR -> LLVM optimization -> Tower foundation -> .towerbc`
the standard compilation path. Optimization is enabled by default; debug/no-opt
mode goes through the same pipeline with optimization disabled. Preserve the
original unoptimized foundation graph view and graph runner for debugging and
differential comparison. Do not introduce a separate home-grown optimizer or a
normal public graph-to-bytecode bypass. The final foundation-to-cache encoder
remains necessary internally and lets the portable loader run without LLVM.

Long-term direction reaffirmed: translate/absorb LLVM into Tower and unify its
applicable operations/optimizations on the shared foundation entity/component
model. The current external LLVM bridge is incremental scaffolding toward that
single environment, not a new authoritative IR or independent bytecode language.
The user explicitly prefers relying on LLVM's optimizations now rather than
writing competing optimizers. The bridge itself still needs correctness checks;
LLVM verification alone cannot prove the return translation is correct.

Current inspection: `backend_optimize` already invokes the upstream pass manager
on the live LLVM module and verifies each pass. The missing implementation is
LLVM-IR inspection and reconstruction of compilable Tower foundation operations.
There is currently no LLVM instruction/block visitor in the backend bindings.
The intended bridge consumes optimized IR directly before native code emission,
retains an explicit VM layout/semantic profile, and lowers SSA merges, control
flow, memory operations and supported intrinsics to shared foundation constructs.
It must reject unsupported constructs explicitly instead of silently shipping
unoptimized output under an optimized label. LLVM may produce unstructured CFGs;
needed control-flow spellings must exist in Foundation and use the same checker,
formatter, graph interpreter, cache compiler and LLVM lowering.

Reference documentation: [LLVM transformation passes](https://llvm.org/docs/Passes.html)
and [LLVM backend structure](https://llvm.org/docs/WritingAnLLVMBackend.html).
This entry records the agreed design and work now starting, not a claim that the
LLVM-to-Tower return path is implemented or validated yet.

Implementation trial (in progress, superseding the missing-visitor observation):
the return translator is now Tower code in backend/import-{bindings,foundation,
values,instructions,module}.tower. It visits LLVM's C API, attaches existing
FoundationNode components to ordinary entities, and uses the shared formatter
and semantic compiler. Phi edges take all incoming snapshots before assigning
destinations. Generated locals precede labels; all reconstructed expressions
remain instruction-like. Runtime calls map to ordinary foundation calls.
Pointers use the selected 4/8-byte target layout, and integer memory accesses
retain their actual LLVM byte width, including narrow legalized integers.

Added foundation calls `label(name)`, `jump(name)` and `trap(message, offset)`.
Labels are function-local direct statements, forward jumps are resolved during
checking, and intermediate labeled blocks must terminate. These are shared
operations supported by checking, formatting, both interpreters and LLVM
lowering. An initial keyword spelling (`label name`) was rejected after it
broke existing fields named `label` in compiler source. Ordinary call spelling
avoids a new reserved lexical keyword. A subsequent label-name bug came from
trying to find token names as parser-rule labels; resolution now uses the
CoreLocation's captured Identifier instead.

Native smoke tests already execute the sum(100) loop as 4950 through optimized
and debug LLVM return paths. The selected initial portable scalar pass profile
is upstream `function(sroa,mem2reg,early-cse,sccp,simplifycfg,dce,lower-switch)`,
with verification and vectorization disabled; it is not the native backend's
full O2 pipeline. No custom constant folding, inlining or peephole optimizer was
added. Unsupported LLVM operations must produce a diagnostic. Future expansion
of the pass profile requires corresponding legality and differential tests.
The first pass spelling `lowerswitch` failed on LLVM 19; the registered spelling
is `lower-switch`. Eligible scalar labeled functions without address operations
place locals/parameters in VM registers and need no guest stack-frame bytes.
This is target register placement, not a substitute for LLVM optimization.

Differential testing found and fixed reconstruction issues in allocation
element types, boolean bitwise legalization, large literal typing and LLVM
truncation. Foundation `convert` checks numeric range, whereas LLVM truncation
discards high bits: the bridge must mask first. Large LLVM constants need typed
locals when passed to calls/conversions because bare Tower literals otherwise
receive the language's default integer type. An explicit trap initially set
failure without setting the fast runner's completion flag, causing a CLI loop
to spin; the explicit-trap path now completes execution as well.

The CLI source fast-run and bytecode producers now call the bridge by default;
`--no-optimize` takes the same lowering/import path with passes disabled. The
worker integration and an enabled-by-default "Optimize with LLVM" control are
being wired through the same API. The direct foundation/cache encoder remains
internal for loading, round-trip checks and reference comparisons. Container
version stays 1; semantics/cache revisions advance to 2 for the added operations
and register placement. Header profile is 0 for an internal reference cache,
1 for the LLVM scalar profile, 2 for the same bridge with passes disabled.

Reproduction environment: Windows checkout, Docker `tower_build`, native LLVM
19, frozen bootstrap `/cache/shared-native/towerc-stage1`, native build
`/cache/fast-backend-native`. Focused command:
`python3 scaffolding/tests/bytecode-llvm.py /cache/fast-backend-native/towerc
build/llvm-bc-tests`. This checks optimized/debug, both pointer widths, original
graph vs imported fast execution, package loading, disassembled graph execution
and deterministic re-encoding. Full validation and performance results are still
pending; successful smoke cases are not a claim that the suite has passed.
Browser LLVM/lld 20 is being built from pinned 1e57ee22 with WASI SDK 34 in
`/cache/llvm-bc-browser`, using the TowerBackend CMake integration. Linux Git
status over the Windows vendor checkout stalled, so after Windows Git confirmed
the vendor checkout was clean, a Windows `git archive` snapshot was extracted
to `/cache/llvm-source`; no upstream source was edited.

Implementation results and superseding optimization decision:

- The standard producer path is now graph -> LLVM -> scalar O2 -> shared
  foundation entities -> canonical foundation -> private execution cache. The
  initial small pass list above was a trial, not the final configuration. The
  final pipeline is `function(sroa,mem2reg),default<O2>,function(lower-switch)`,
  with verification after each pass, loop/SLP vectorization disabled and no
  native target machine supplied to these portable interpreter passes. The VM
  still has an explicit wasm32/wasm64 data layout. Debug uses this same bridge
  with optimization passes disabled. LLVM performs the semantic optimizations;
  Tower performs representation/legalization and register placement.
- The CLI and browser fast target use that path by default. The playground's
  "Optimize with LLVM" checkbox persists its state and controls both cache and
  compiled targets. The original graph display/runner remains available. The
  two LLVM panes also remain visible for a fast-only selection. Downloaded
  `.towerbc` contains the reconstructed, compilable foundation, with container
  version 1, semantics/cache revisions 2 and profile 1 (O2) or 2 (no passes).
  Internal profile 0 is retained for the reference encoder and loader checks;
  it is not an exposed source-compilation bypass. The final encoder cannot be
  removed: the loader reconstructs and verifies the execution cache without LLVM.
- The importer preserves external/exported function types (signedness, bool,
  usize width and nominal struct pointers) from their original foundation
  entities. Normalizing public signatures to LLVM's unsigned bit representation
  initially changed host marshalling, including JS Number versus BigInt. That
  was incorrect. A follow-up boolean case exposed invalid `bits(bool, ...)`;
  booleans now use their numeric conversion contract. Internal temporary types
  remain legal scalar representations. Exact reserved runtime names replace a
  prefix filter that incorrectly discarded a user export called `tower_user`.
- Foundation labels/jumps represent arbitrary LLVM CFGs; phi copies snapshot
  incoming values before any destination changes. These are ordinary shared
  operations with compilable spellings, not an independent bytecode semantic
  model. Narrow integer memory accesses use their exact byte extent. Integer
  truncation masks before checked Foundation conversion. Signed comparisons,
  GEP indices, globals, static stack storage, memory intrinsics and allocation
  product overflow retain explicit target width and bit semantics.
- Existing checked numeric conversion lowering used synthetic i128 comparisons.
  It now checks the <=64-bit Foundation domain directly using appropriate signed
  or unsigned bounds. Boundary fixtures cover i64/u64, i32/u32, u8, bool and
  usize under both pointer widths, including failing conversions. CLI runtime
  trap coordinates are resolved against the original input rather than the
  generated foundation text; multi-line trap tests compare the full diagnostic.
  Imported/generated instructions still do not claim fabricated source spans.

Performance experiments and root causes (exploratory timings are not final
cross-trial speedup claims): the first LLVM return path was often slower than
both the raw cache and graph runner. The conservative first register-placement
rule excluded an entire function if any address occurred. This kept LLVM SSA
locals in guest memory, defeating the intended compact register execution.
Placement now checks each local: scalar locals/parameters remain in VM registers
unless that local's address escapes; addressed/aggregate storage keeps its
original layout. Read-only operands use their persistent register directly;
operations produce a fresh result rather than clobbering that operand. Pure
register functions need zero guest stack-frame bytes. Build-time lookup indexes
are released after cache construction; they are not stored in the opcode stream.

The small-pass trial still left large amounts of guest work and made memory and
branch workloads slower. Scalar O2 improved arithmetic, calls and branches, but
memory remained slow. Inspection found a constant LLVM shift being expanded
into six runtime exponentiation branches. Constant shifts now lower directly to
multiply/divide by the known power of two. GEP sign extension is needed only
when the index is narrower than the pointer; same-width modular arithmetic no
longer takes the expensive widening path. These are lowering choices, not a
second optimizer. The final measured workloads use no wide instructions.

An additional valid absolute-value program exposed an O2 legality gap:
InstCombine produced `llvm.abs.i32`, which the importer diagnosed as unsupported.
The translator now legalizes absolute value and unsigned/signed saturating
add/subtract using Foundation scalar operations. The new 32/64-bit fixtures
obtain a zero from an opaque platform call and derive arguments from it, so
LLVM cannot fold the tested runtime operations to constants. Tests also inspect
optimized IR to establish whether the intended intrinsic was actually exercised.
Other unsupported IR is diagnosed explicitly; there is no silent raw-cache
fallback that would mislabel a program as optimized.

Verification/debugging notes: a native differential run launched while the linker
was replacing its compiler executable failed with PermissionError. That trial
is invalid and was repeated after the build finished. Canonical-format checks
also caught unformatted in-progress Tower edits; all edited Tower files were
formatted with the shared engine before final validation. The original browser
run passed 122/130: four expectations failed in both viewport configurations.
They assumed original function names survived O2, LLVM panes disappeared with
Wasm disabled, only one worker would load LLVM, and the timing list had no fast
LLVM phase. The updated assertions check the original graph separately, check
optimized compilable foundation and profile-tagged downloads, and preserve the
Wasm worker reuse check. A test interaction also needed to reopen the Targets
popover after an outside download click. Focused corrected cases pass.

Benchmark harness correction: Wasm's final update callback contains only the
latest streamed output chunk; comparing that to the whole reference loses
output on runs lasting more than 50 ms. Benchmarks now compare the complete
`executeWasm` result. The initial profile's arithmetic sum was eliminated by O2
and yielded a single useful sample. The profiling workload now XORs each
accumulated sum so there is sustained runtime work. Profiling is separate from
benchmark timing. Final samples, complete validation and publication are recorded
below when finished.

Reference checks on 2026-11-19 used upstream documentation for
[transformation passes](https://llvm.org/docs/Passes.html),
[phi edge semantics](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#phi-instruction), and
[loop/SLP vectorization](https://llvm.org/docs/Vectorizers.html). Disabling the two
vectorizers is an explicit scalar legality choice, not a claim that arbitrary
LLVM IR is accepted or that O2 produces globally optimal interpreter code.

Final legality tests also exposed excessive generated module scope in debug mode:
bytewise global initializers had placed every temporary at module scope,
exceeding the frontend's 1,024 top-level construct budget for a small source
program with several conversion diagnostics. Initialization now runs in a
generated ordinary function; its temporaries occupy a temporary function frame,
while actual globals retain their module identity and initialization order. This
also avoids permanently reserving guest global memory for initializer scratch.
The public frontend limit was not raised to conceal generated-code growth.

The first opaque-input test used an incorrect platform_write prototype (usize
return instead of the documented i64) and therefore failed compiled Wasm host
marshalling. Correcting the fixture to the library's u32/u8*/usize -> i64
contract resolved that harness failure. The signed bitwise overflow idiom was
not recognized as a saturation intrinsic by this LLVM profile. For i32, the
fixture now uses widened arithmetic and range clamping, following upstream
llvm/test/Transforms/InstCombine/sadd_sat.ll; assertions confirm sadd/ssub.sat
are produced. The i64 signed bitwise cases remain differential checks without
a false claim of intrinsic recognition. All 37 focused LLVM execution tests
then passed, including both optimized and debug reconstruction.

Final validation before publication:

- `python3 scaffolding/tests/bytecode-llvm.py /cache/fast-backend-native/towerc build/llvm-bc-final-tests`: **172** comparisons passed (43 sources x two pointer widths x optimized/debug), each including original graph execution, imported cache execution, package load, disassembled graph execution and deterministic regeneration. The final source set includes the corrected runtime-input scalar idioms. Full source-file diagnostics, not just error messages, agree for the trap cases.
- `python3 scaffolding/tests/interpreter-llvm.py`: **16** compiled native optimized/unoptimized comparisons passed. The Tower backend API harness passed after the final importer rebuild.
- `npm test --prefix playground`: **252/252**, no skips. `npm run test:browser --prefix playground`: **130/130**, desktop and mobile Chromium, after the final artifact build. Includes cancellation, stale-result rejection, editable grammars, all targets, independent runners, optimized/debug cache downloads and persistence.
- Windows native parser/formatter suite passed; **147** Tower sources are canonical. Windows interpreter differential **156** passed. WASI interpreter differential **156** passed. ASAN/UBSAN host/adapter build: **5/5** CTest passed. Generated Tower object code itself is not sanitizer-instrumented. The last importer-only additions were checked by the rebuilt native/browser LLVM suites above; they do not change those interpreter/host objects.
- `npm run check:format --prefix playground` and `git diff --check` passed. `npm run test:deployment --prefix playground` verified all **36** local deployment asset hashes plus both browser configurations, three-runner agreement, current cache revisions/profile, project persistence, native downloads and platform defaults.

Final measurements are archived with all samples, cache statistics, environment,
artifact hashes and named profile summaries in
[2026-11-19-llvm-bytecode.json](research/2026-11-19-llvm-bytecode.json).
The timing runs were sequential after builds and browser tests stopped, on AMD
Ryzen AI MAX+ 395. Each workload uses three warmups and 15 measured samples;
interpreter order alternates. Windows Node 21.7.3/V8 executes the Wasm-hosted
interpreters; native Linux x64 uses LLVM 19 in Docker with Node 22.23.5 driving
the CLI. Do not compare these two environments as a controlled host comparison.

| Workload | Graph ms | Raw cache ms | LLVM O2 cache ms | LLVM debug cache ms | Compiled Wasm ms |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Arithmetic | 4.2805 | 1.1257 | 0.9204 | 3.4244 | 0.2136 |
| Calls | 2.9689 | 0.7070 | 0.0146 | 1.6988 | 0.2257 |
| Memory | 5.6455 | 2.0062 | 1.7692 | 8.4236 | 0.2476 |
| Branches | 7.3604 | 2.2472 | 2.0324 | 12.0464 | 0.2896 |

Excluding the calls workload that O2 largely eliminates, the optimized cache is
**3.19�4.65x** faster than the graph runner and **1.11�1.22x** faster than the raw
cache in this Wasm-hosted sample. The calls result measures eliminated guest
work, not 203x better dispatch. Compiled Wasm remains faster on the three
sustained-work workloads; its measured path includes fresh instantiation and
host execution, so these are not steady-state inner-loop timings. Debug is
intentionally the same LLVM bridge without simplification and can be slower
than the original graph. An interpreter is not claimed to outperform native
compiled execution generally.

Native CLI execution graph/O2-cache medians (ms): arithmetic **1.51341/0.45749**,
calls **1.07698/0.020008**, memory **2.32484/1.28000**, branches
**2.07802/0.692675**. The three sustained-work cases improve **1.82�3.31x**.
LLVM guest compilation is an upfront cost: Wasm-hosted compilation/import took
approximately **21�170 ms** in these one-off measurements (the first case also
warms the compiler); subsequent foundation compile/cache preparation medians
were **3.36�4.85 ms**. These are separate from execution. Optimized code occupied
**84�556 bytes**, cache capacity **724�2,108 bytes**, and register capacity
**64�408 bytes**, with **zero wide instructions** in these fixtures. Those are
hot-cache metrics, not total package or process memory. Canonical foundation,
validation graphs, guest memory, compiler reactors and worker copies still cost
memory. The format is not advertised as a zero-overhead public VM product.

The graph profile remains dominated by interpreter scheduling, operand readiness,
component-cache lookup and task pushing. Raw cache sampling shifts to dispatch,
loads/stores and calls. LLVM cache sampling puts **94.4%** of sampled hits in
`fast_interpreter_step`, with the remaining material guest work in scalar
arithmetic; call and local-load/store overhead nearly disappears on this
workload. The earlier graph lookup/call-buffer/memory improvements remain in
place; this turn extends graph semantics for reconstructed CFGs and profiles
both paths again. No additional graph speedup is claimed from this measurement.

Inspection of `llvm-objdump-19 --disassemble-symbols=fast_interpreter_step --no-show-raw-insn /cache/fast-backend-native/tower-compiler-interpreter.o`
shows one packed 32-bit instruction load and byte/shift extraction on x64;
the Wasm object uses unsigned shifts/masks and br_table dispatch. LLVM chooses
these machine details when compiling the Tower interpreter. No handwritten
x86/ARM instructions, C-return-register ABI tricks, guest JIT or executable
memory allocation were introduced. Physical ARM, macOS, iPhone and console
performance remains unmeasured. The explicit scalar legality boundary still
rejects unsupported intrinsics/types, atomic/volatile memory, dynamic allocas
and over-aligned storage; extending that boundary requires differential tests.
Explicit trap messages have a nonempty, readable NUL-terminated-string contract.
Package disassembly preserves the numeric diagnostic payload, but a package
cannot reconstruct original source text that was not stored in it.

Arithmetic, memory and branch workloads show 3.66-4.58x graph-to-O2-cache speedup
and 1.09-1.26x raw-cache-to-O2-cache speedup. O2 largely eliminates the calls
workload, so its ratio is not dispatch throughput. Compiled Wasm remains faster
on sustained work; those timings include fresh instantiation and host execution.
No-opt intentionally retains lowering work and can be slower than the original
graph runner. LLVM optimization is separate: 16.5-164.5 ms here (first workload
includes warming); subsequent cache preparation is 0.27-1.41 ms. These are small
programs, not a universal startup or large-program scaling guarantee.

arithmetic 1.880270/0.792797; calls 1.279440/0.025168; memory 2.834370/1.698320; branch 2.447350/0.985890.

combine native and Wasm-hosted ratios into one platform-independent guarantee.

## 2026-11-19 - Cursor LR completion and shared semantic resolution

The reported `print(va` popup showed both `value` and the statement keyword `var`. The previous completion implementation enumerated every active literal and guessed roles from punctuation; it did not check the LR stack at the replacement boundary. That earlier scope/type limitation is superseded by the implementation below.

Implemented an opt-in recognizer snapshot immediately after the lexer reports EOF and before EOF reductions alter its stack. Tower-owned LR probes simulate candidate shifts with the complete stack, reductions and gotos; inspecting a top-state action row alone is insufficient. The syntax adapter retains the corresponding grammar revision and uses the current Tower lexer to validate concrete candidate spellings. Keyword candidates use their actual literal IDs, so the declaration literal `var` is rejected inside call arguments even though Identifier is legal there. Function candidates additionally require an accepted Identifier followed by the current grammar's opening-call literal. Completed declaration boundaries use the next construct's initial state; declarations after the caret do not affect eligibility.

The Tower query prefers the real source suffix and constructs a disposable ordinary parse snapshot with a lexically valid identifier hole identified by source coordinates, never by a reserved name. For incomplete edits, a deterministic LR probe first tries closing tokens, then falls back to a breadth-first continuation search (512 paths, 24 tokens, 65,536 probe actions; individual candidate checks have 8,192 actions and the probe's 128-reduction cap; both continuation strategies share the same action budget). This is recovery source, not another AST, instruction language or stored program format. The full snapshot and any later/project declarations become ordinary shared entities with source-base metadata. A narrow optional SemanticEditor observer in the existing semantic resolver captures the actual scope, expected FoundationType and resolved member receiver. The ordinary compiler remains unchanged when that observer is absent. Completed bodies of unrelated functions are skipped in an editor query.

Removed the previous syntactic declaration collector, annotation-string receiver matching and colon/dot role guesses. Completion now enumerates the compiler's derived name/scope tables over those same entities, honors shadowing before type filtering, uses nominal FoundationType equality, and resolves inferred locals, nested fields, arrays, address/load operands, function signatures, returns, conditions and assignments. Builtin editor argument observation uses the existing operation identities/arity and ordinary type/value helpers, including incomplete type/count/byte/pointer argument lists. Void calls are excluded from value positions; type objects and boolean/null literals are filtered by semantic role. The browser adapter is smaller and retains only transport, session and grammar-vocabulary access; completion, LR search and semantic resolution execute as compiled .tower in the worker Wasm module. Native syntax/table adapters still exist in the broader bootstrap compiler.

Trials and fixes: initial bootstrap compilation rejected reserved field names (`expected`, `token`) and comparison expressions directly in `if`; switched to ordinary boolean locals. Passing an LRCompletionPath by value through vector_push hit the bootstrap's unsupported aggregate-copy path and segfaulted; switched to the existing pointer-based lr_append, preserving raw Foundation pointer semantics. A final nested-block stress check found that breadth-first recovery exhausted its path budget exploring new statements before closing even one extra block. Added a closure-preference pass with the same LR legality checks and budget, retaining breadth-first fallback; regression tests cover one, three and six unfinished nested blocks. Unwritten function signature tails now use the shared Foundation void type spelling for scratch recovery, allowing parameter and return type suggestions before the body exists. Tests caught a shadowed outer variable leaking through when the inner binding failed type filtering, a load observer losing its expected pointer type in recursive operand resolution, and void builtins appearing in print arguments; all were corrected. Initial test expectations were corrected where valid alternatives existed (e.g. convert can produce a usize count, and extending Statement retains alloc/alignof alongside a new alpha keyword).

Validation environment: Windows Node 21.7.3 and Chromium Playwright desktop/Pixel 7 projects; WSL Orchestral-Revng, WASI SDK 34 and /root/.cache/tower/native/towerc-stage1. Commands: cmake --build build/browser-wasi --parallel 4; node --test playground/tests/completion.test.mjs; Tower's own formatter over the six changed Tower modules with idempotence and parse-tree checks; playground/scripts/test-native-core.sh with ASan/UBSan. Detailed final suite and publication results are recorded below.

Remaining limits: recovery and candidate lists are bounded (128 results); sufficiently broken preceding declarations, an unresolvable type, or exhaustion of the continuation budget can yield no semantic suggestions rather than a broad unrelated list. Generic candidates requiring unsupplied type arguments and arbitrary custom semantic operations do not acquire invented type information. This is a shared-resolver completion service, not a claim that every possible malformed edit has a complete language-server answer.

The final native ASan/UBSan build passed all 5 CTest targets. Tower formatting was idempotent and preserved parsed structure for all six edited Tower modules. The final local deployment verifier matched all 38 assets and passed desktop/mobile parser/type popup assertions, all execution backends, native target downloads, project persistence and uniform output/highlighting checks. ## 2026-11-19 - Completion latency and a diagnostic typing grace period

The request was to reduce the actual dot-keystroke-to-suggestion latency and defer new errors until ten seconds of idle input or cursor departure. Measured the browser path before changing it: CodeMirror's default 100 ms activation debounce accounted for roughly 103-113 ms before the worker request. On Windows, Ryzen 9 5900HX, Node v21.7.3 and Playwright Chromium (desktop 1440x1000 and Pixel 7 emulation), 20 repeated dot/backspace samples gave warm median 141.7/140.1 ms and p95 160.0/150.3 ms. First dots after the same 400 ms editing pause took 254.5/286.7 ms because they also started the language worker. The standalone Wasm query remained roughly 35-49 ms, so HTML painting was not the dominant original cost.

Added playground/scripts/benchmark-completion.mjs. It records the real dot keydown, worker send/reply, popup DOM mutation, correct visible labels and an after-requestAnimationFrame task as a conservative paint boundary. This does not measure physical monitor presentation or establish a universal zero-millisecond guarantee. The default scenario repeats dots without an inter-keystroke pause; --settled changes field declarations on every sample and waits 150 ms before the dot, ruling out replay of a previous declaration's answer. Commands: node playground/scripts/benchmark-completion.mjs http://127.0.0.1:4173/ build/completion-latency-immediate.json and the same with build/completion-latency-prepared.json --settled. Raw initial evidence: build/completion-latency-{before,step1,immediate,prepared}.json and build/completion-latency-wasm.log.

Removed the activation and acceptance interaction delays and warm the completion worker on editor focus. A single bounded prediction asks the ordinary Tower/Wasm completion query about inserting a dot after 80 ms of quiet input. It includes the entire suffix and exact module/grammar environment, normalizing the active file to that projected source. Reuse requires byte-for-byte input identity and cursor identity; it is not a JavaScript name/type/member table. The same LR tables, ordinary type resolver and ECS entities determine every option. A mismatched edit, selection, file or environment cancels the prediction; blur and editor destruction clear it. The foreground request can share a matching in-flight prediction. This trades one idle speculative query for removing a later worker round trip; it does not claim less total compiler work for every typing pattern. A missed prediction still queries immediately and rejects stale replies.

Initial timings after these changes: repeated uncached dots had warm medians 41.3/40.8 ms and p95 44.0/43.2 ms; varied, prepared answers had medians 14.6/30.9 ms and p95 21.7/36.0 ms at the conservative paint boundary, with zero worker requests after the dot in those prepared samples. These are local observations, not hardware-independent guarantees. Final post-integration measurements are recorded separately below.

DiagnosticDelay gates presentation rather than compilation. Each focused edit resets a ten-second timer and discards pending errors from the older revision. Successful analysis/compilation clears obsolete errors immediately. Newly reported editor and execution-pane errors remain pending until idle, a selection-only cursor move, blur or explicit Execute. Old visible diagnostics remain mapped while typing until a fresh successful result clears them. File switches reset the gate and show that file's current errors normally. Source parsing/execution retain the existing 200 ms quiet period; they do not wait ten seconds. The revision/generation guards reject late results.

Experiments caught two issues before publication. Calling browser setTimeout/clearTimeout as methods of the injected timer owner caused Illegal invocation; wrapper functions preserve the platform receiver. More substantially, using the same LanguageService coalescing key for a foreground completion and a prediction could discard the visible query during a slow first load or delayed worker reply. Predictions now have their own bounded queue key. Added a 400 ms worker-load regression and retained the 600 ms delayed-reply regression. The execution-worker reuse test was also narrowed to finish completion's independent initial load before asserting that execution performs no new Wasm fetch. A deployment assertion incorrectly expected all errors hidden after selecting an older invalid fixture; selecting all intentionally reveals that fixture's pending error. It now starts from valid source before asserting suppression of a new error.

Pre-integration validation: 285 Node/Wasm tests passed before the queue regression was added; all eight final timer/prediction unit cases pass. All 16 final desktop/mobile completion checks and both execution-worker reuse checks pass. The full browser matrix and final deployment verification are recorded below. Existing error fixtures now explicitly move the cursor when requesting immediate diagnostics, while new clock-controlled browser tests verify the exact 10,000 ms boundary, timer restart, independent background analysis, semantic/output suppression, cursor/blur release, correction and document-switch invalidation. The source and instruction highlighting path remains shared and is covered by the existing browser comparisons.

## 2026-11-19 — Continue the full language roadmap; shared parallel compiler core

After the first milestone, the user explicitly requested all remaining language
work and asked that ECS/Burst-style processing underpin the entire compiler so
large amounts of Tower can compile across threads. This is continuing work, not
a claim that the first milestone completed the roadmap. main was pulled/rebased
again and was current at 014fdbf.

The plan now includes a cross-cutting compiler execution architecture: cached
component queries, compact derived work/dependency indexes, immutable published
revisions, explicit access sets, task-owned scratch/results, deterministic commits,
and serial/native/browser executors. Result propagation remains ordinary typed
branches/returns on shared entities. No GC or exceptions; no independent semantic
IR and no new owned native implementation.

Audit finding: library/entities.tower currently uses unsynchronized next_id,
entity/component counts and reference counts, and mutable per-type instance arrays.
Its comments explicitly invalidate query cursors on structural edits.
compiler/host-entities.tower still receives a singleton compiler_entity_store()
through the existing host boundary. These are real prerequisites for in-process
parallel mutation, not already-thread-safe infrastructure. Stable component
addresses and per-type queries do provide a starting point for cached batches.
The plan requires storage/cache/allocator isolation and deterministic publication
before enabling concurrent writers, plus scale/determinism/race/cancellation tests.

Read primary references: https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/Queries.html and
https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/Systems.html (the old Multithreading.html URL failed),
and https://docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.burst@1.8/manual/index.html .
Flecs documents cached queries and systems with access declarations; Burst compiles
compatible code/jobs through LLVM. Tower will adopt applicable data-oriented
principles in its own shared-node compiler, not claim Flecs/Burst integration.

Next implementation work begins with nominal enum/type identity and result-value
prerequisites while retaining this whole-compiler architecture. Full returned
errors, demand resolution, parallel execution and the other requested language
features remain active work.

### Nominal enums and the first shared work-graph consumer

Implemented nominal integer-backed enums on the original declaration/member
entities. Foundation has an explicit-discriminant spelling; tower.tower adds
omitted discriminants. The existing type representation retains its nominal
record identity alongside the integer scalar representation, so LLVM/interpreter
storage and external layout remain the selected target's integer layout without
adding a second type registry or native ABI field. Named members are constants,
not addressable locations. Exact enum equality is allowed; implicit integer or
cross-enum conversions, arithmetic and enum indexing are rejected. Explicit
integer conversion can produce unnamed values, so match still requires `_`.
Forward discriminant expressions/flags/closed-enum exhaustiveness are unfinished.
Canonical Foundation prints the nominal type and all explicit discriminants.
Completion reads the same enum/member declarations and respects lexical shadowing.

Added library/work-graph.tower entirely in Tower, using nominal WorkState and
WorkError enums. Queries are deduplicated by exact subject/query/argument keys in
an explicit revision/profile. Dense task/edge arrays and hash indexes are derived
data over borrowed entities. Dependency and consumer links share one edge entry;
duplicate reads do not allocate duplicate edges. Demand discovery, failed-input
propagation and cycle-path detection are iterative. Ready tickets allow bounded
batches; completion validates revision/profile/state, and cancellation rejects
outstanding results. The coordinator exclusively mutates this index. Worker-owned
payloads, access-conflict checks, real thread executors and incremental invalidation
are not implemented by these functions. They do not make EntityStore thread safe.

The semantic compiler now uses this common core for layout dependency discovery
and execution. A layout kernel reads completed dependency layouts and writes its
type size/alignment and field offsets; it does not recursively discover work.
Pointer fields do not demand pointee layout. Completed queries are reused across
the compilation. This removes the layout recursion limit and the prototype
256-type/field caps, with hashed name lookup, growable indexed storage and the
existing compilation node/storage budgets still in force. Other recursive type
construction/inference limits are not silently removed. Layout errors now include
the actual by-value cycle chain.

Bootstrap trial: copied the verified enum-capable Tower-built native compiler to
the ignored build/import-port/towerc staging path (saved its predecessor as
build/language-next/towerc-before-enums). Compiler modules now use Tower enums and
while directly; no new native seed/implementation was added. The staged compiler
must receive explicit --bedrock/--foundation paths: its old adjacent share/tower
directory otherwise selects an older grammar. CMake already passes those paths.

### Cross-target runtime contracts exposed by the larger work fixture

The full cross-target trial exposed two pre-existing gaps in the restricted target
support packs. Windows large stack frames referenced __chkstk, absent from the
small kernel32 import library. Disabling stack probes would violate guard-page
behavior. LLVM's pinned X86TargetLowering::hasInlineStackProbe explicitly excludes
Windows, so applying probe-stack="inline-asm" is not a valid fix there. Microsoft
documents the existing OS export in kernelbase.dll:
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/devnotes/-win32-__chkstk .
LLVM attribute reference: https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#function-attributes .

Added a Tower COFF short-import/archive metadata writer and a lazy __chkstk import
to the link plan. Upstream LLD supplies the import thunk; the OS supplies the stack
probe with its required nonstandard register contract. This is metadata, not a
Tower/C/C++ implementation pretending to be __chkstk. The lazy archive avoids
adding the OS import when no probe is needed and follows user-supplied libraries.
Format source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/debug/pe-format .
The existing package/build scripts and native wrappers were not changed.

Darwin zero-fill lowering similarly referenced __bzero on x64 and bzero on ARM64,
which the minimal libSystem description omitted. The Tower linker now generates
a supplementary TAPI description for those existing libSystem exports, with
architecture-specific symbol lists. A trial confirmed LLD merges it with the
supplied SDK description. The first generated trial lacked a final newline and
TAPI rejected its document terminator; the generated Tower string includes one.
No implementation is hidden under third_party and no additional runtime library
is introduced. Object-only consumers retain responsibility for their target ABI
support libraries, as before.

The new upstream interpreter pipeline exposed a size regression: the work-graph

65,536 Foundation-node budget at both pointer widths. Optimized reconstruction
already passed. The initial attempt to emit LLVM constants as bare operands was
rejected: bits/convert infer their source operand type independently, so literal

Implemented reconstruction reductions entirely in Tower, without changing the
resource limit or enabling LLVM passes in the raw profile:

- Reuse one typed, initialized local per distinct LLVM constant within a function.
  Its initializer precedes the function's blocks, so a use in a later branch does
  not depend on another branch executing. Clear the derived association index at
  each function boundary; retain no new semantic authority outside shared nodes.
- Address-of fixed storage is already a Foundation operand, so it needs no extra
  local before its pointer conversion.
- Every LLVM instruction already owns a result local for forward references.
  Reuse it for the final newly generated temporary when its type matches exactly
  and the final statement assigns that temporary. Do not coalesce existing values,
  shared literals, branch results or different types. This preserves evaluation
  order while removing a redundant declaration/copy from reconstructed text.

## 2026-11-19 - Direct Tower language queries and cached hover inspection

The follow-up request was IDE-style mouse hover for types and underlying nodes, sharing the completion query machinery and keeping the native/Wasm path directly linked. Added compiler/language-query.tower with exported language_document/language_document_result and the existing completion_dispose lifetime. The implementation reuses CompletionQuery's module loading, baseline selection, temporary source ownership, ordinary semantic context, type resolver and real entity/component relationships. It walks the ordered syntax hierarchy, selects the checked binding/type/field, and returns disposable source-range presentation records. JavaScript does no name lookup, parsing or type inference. Snapshot entity IDs, parent IDs, component counts, bound entities, type layout and field offsets come from the actual shared nodes. Imported definitions contribute bindings without leaking their foreign source offsets into the active editor.

Signatures use the existing canonical formatter. Extracted its shared FormatResult/FormatSpan declarations into format-types.tower and reused a single function-header formatter for both whole-program output and the new format_summary display fragment. A summary is explicitly a display fragment, not a new program interchange format. Grammar-changing roots are retained for inspection without adding grammar declarations to the executable statement list. The query rejects invalid UTF-8/NUL input, more than 8 MiB, invalid baseline modes and unsupported pointer widths; traversal is bounded to depth 256 and 100,000 visited nodes, and parsing retains the existing 1,024-boundary limit. Layout follows the explicit 4/8-byte target profile. All query-owned entities/output are released after the host copies JSON; repeated-query tests verify stable live node/allocation counts. These are Tower functions compiled into the existing native and Wasm semantic unit, with no additional native query adapter or language-server process. Transitional native parser/platform dependencies elsewhere in the compiler remain; this is not a claim that the entire compiler is already pure Tower.

Browser completion and inspection share LanguageService, languagePayload and the selected compiler/module environment. A 150 ms quiet period prepares one exact document index; mouse movement over a ready index performs only a range lookup and tooltip rendering. The cache includes source/environment/compiler revision, invalidates on edits/file changes, and rejects stale asynchronous results. Compiler changes close tooltips and invalidate the index. The tooltip uses textContent, shows signatures, inferred types, return types, layouts and ECS metadata, and marks entity identifiers as snapshot-local. CodeMirror's installed hover implementation uses options.hoverTime || 300, so zero would restore its 300 ms default; configured 1 ms, the smallest usable built-in trigger. A cancelled/null response is retryable instead of permanently caching a missing result.

Keystrokes take priority over queued background inspection. A measured cold inspection of units/compiler-parser-nodes.tower with the full compiler project's import closure took 3,009 ms; compiler/completion.tower took 80 ms, and both returned syntax-only information in that environment. This exposed an important scheduling limitation: queue priority cannot interrupt an already executing synchronous Wasm call. When foreground completion arrives during inspection, it now gives that call 16 ms to finish, then replaces the worker and resolves the discarded document query as cancelled. Pending completion is preserved and dispatched first. Small completed calls keep their warm worker; expensive background work cannot add its entire remaining runtime to a keystroke. This trades a new worker/instance for bounded waiting on the old inspection, not a universal 16 ms completion guarantee. Tests cover priority, worker replacement and a real browser worker with inspection replies deliberately delayed 2.5 seconds.

Error recovery deliberately avoids guessed types. A syntactically unfinished suffix can retain checked earlier declarations; if ordinary semantic checking fails, the snapshot exposes syntax/entity metadata without inferred types. It does not yet provide full language-server-style local recovery inside every incomplete function or resolve every compiler source file outside its complete build unit. First uncached inspection and large import closures still cost compiler work. The disposable range index is not an authoritative semantic model or persistent entity handle store.

Implementation trials: the first Tower build rejected general comparison conditions and an inline depth + 1 call argument under the instruction-like foundation grammar; lowered those through ordinary typed locals and ran the shared formatter with idempotence/tree-preservation checks. A direct LLVM CMake regeneration encountered upstream config.guess CRLF; the established build-llvm.sh normalizes/restores those upstream scripts and rebuilt both reactors successfully. Used the published Tower/Wasm compiler as the import-capable bootstrap through build/context-bootstrap.sh. Rebuilt the compiler project recipe with the official package-compiler-project.py from actual parser/LLVM build manifests, including the new source files, semantic-unit import and exports. Candidate compiler validation now requires typed hover as well as completion, imports, interpreters, LLVM and native target output.

All 48 desktop/mobile completion, hover, delayed-diagnostic, interaction and output-highlighting browser cases passed before the interruption regression was added. All five native ASAN-configured CTests passed in 135.94 s (the generated Tower objects are not themselves ASAN-instrumented). The local deployment verifier matched all 66 assets and passed desktop/mobile execution, imports, grammar editing, target builds/downloads, persistence, completion and compiler-workbench checks. ## 2026-11-19: real compiler workers and component access contracts (plan)

Pulled/rebased main through 6348c3c before work. Continue the complete language
roadmap, prioritizing actual parallel compilation rather than treating the serial
work graph as its completion. The first executor will compile the compiler's own
Tower import units in isolated Wasm instances on real browser/Node worker threads.
Tower owns the dependency graph, concurrency bound, tickets and result acceptance;
JavaScript is worker/message/artifact transport. Inputs are immutable per build,
each worker owns its entities, LLVM context, allocator and filesystem, and reactor
link/publication order remains deterministic. Cancellation must terminate child
workers and reject late results. Compare 1/2/4/8 workers and exact output bytes.

Extend the shared Tower scheduler with declared component read/write ranges and
structural exclusivity. These declarations describe access to existing entities,
not a second semantic graph. Validate overlapping readers, disjoint writes,
conflicts, stale completions and cancellation in Tower fixtures. This is a
contract for future frozen-world kernels, not permission to race current entity
reference counts or mutable type-instance indexes. Current stable sparse payloads
and dense per-type pointer indexes are not packed SIMD columns. Native in-process
workers, shared-node phase migration and measured vectorization remain separate
required milestones; isolated compilation does not claim to complete them.

Implemented the first real executor in `library/compiler-work.tower`, imported
by the existing Tower backend reactor. It owns the work graph, concurrency bound,
unit/join queries, revision/profile validation, cancellation and earliest failing
unit ordinal. Browser/Node adapters transfer a compiled Wasm module plus immutable
source snapshots into isolated worker instances and transfer owned object bytes
back. They do not reimplement dependency resolution or language semantics. All
objects settle before deterministic recipe-order publication/linking; a failed
build publishes none. The browser defaults to at most two workers. The reusable
host API accepts 1 through 8, or serial execution with the same Tower coordinator.
No C/C++ source was added or edited. `cmake/TowerBackend.cmake` only connects the
new Tower exports through the existing isolated backend integration fragment.

The common `work-graph` now accepts component access declarations with explicit
domain/type identities and half-open ranges. Read/read overlap and disjoint writes
are admitted together; a structural lease excludes the entire domain. Conflicting
ready tasks remain queued and stale completions cannot release a live lease.
Scratch, entity lifetime and all structural publication remain executor duties.
Access exclusion is not semantic ordering: dependencies must describe observable
order. Private compiler instances need no shared component leases. Shared-node
layout remains serial; no concurrent world mutation is enabled by this change.

Research confirms the distinction we must preserve. Flecs' documented threaded
systems divide query matches into slices, with stable assignment until a sync
point ([Systems](https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/Systems.html#threading)). This does
not make arbitrary structural changes safe. Burst's
[loop vectorization guidance](https://docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.burst@1.8/manual/optimization-loop-vectorization.html)
shows why aliasing and control flow need separate inspection from worker counts.
The [HTML worker lifecycle](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/workers.html)
provides the browser transport/termination contract; browser tests also inspect
actual nested worker targets on cancellation. No GC, exception mechanism, managed
runtime or external ECS implementation was added to Tower.

The first expanded raw LLVM round-trip trials failed the old global 65,536-node
limit (`parallel-fixtures.log` initially, subsequently overwritten by the passing
rerun). Reduced typed reconstruction from the preceding checkpoint was intact;
the larger scheduler library simply crossed that fixed count. Semantic checking
now has `semantic_compile_budget(..., component_bytes)` and a named 64 MiB default
for newly attached payload accounting in `sem_node`, derived from the real
FoundationNode size. This is not a total-heap limit: existing nodes, parser state,
generated/backend nodes and scratch have other ownership/resource contracts.
Do not infer million-declaration support from this change. The existing entry
point delegates to the explicit budget API; no native ABI layout was extended.
Both pointer widths now pass raw/optimized Foundation reconstruction without
disabling checks or applying optimization to the raw profile.

Functional fixtures are Tower: `work-access` tests read/write/structural conflicts,
disjoint domains/ranges, cancellation, stale tickets and overflow; `compiler-work`
tests bounded dispatch, reverse completion, duplicate/wrong-profile receipts and
source-order failure selection. `parallel-unit` is an exported dense integer
kernel; `compiler-batch` checks zero length, a non-vector-width tail, guards and
modular arithmetic. The first transport test incorrectly tried to compile the
executable language fixtures as libraries; the compiler correctly rejected their
top-level statements. Replaced that test input with the exported Tower kernel.
The first batch fixture also used the grammar token `expected` as a local name;
renaming it `wanted` fixed the parse error. No parser workaround was introduced.

## 2026-11-19 - Translucent immediate hover with per-symbol dwell and tolerant holding

The user requested a pointer-following, click-through preview that becomes opaque and interactive after remaining over the same symbol, including while the pointer moves. Implemented this presentation policy in playground/src/hover.mjs and style.css: 76% preview opacity, an 800 ms continuous dwell on the same source occurrence, then full opacity and a frozen pointer anchor. The solid panel remains while the pointer is over its original symbol, the panel itself, or a rectangle expanded on each side by 25% of the panel width/height. Leaving that area dismisses it; another underlying symbol may immediately start a new preview. Switching symbols restarts dwell. Source/selection changes, Escape, outside clicks, scrolling outside the panel, resize, actual window blur, visibility loss and compiler changes dismiss it and cancel pending dwell/query presentation. Text can be selected/copied inside the solid panel.

CodeMirror's built-in hover helper uses pointer stillness and a fixed four-pixel keep zone, so it could not express this policy. Replaced only that controller using public StateField/showTooltip/repositionTooltips APIs; CodeMirror still owns viewport clamping and placement. Actual DOM Range rectangles distinguish tokens from adjacent blank space and support wrapped ranges. Cached ranges avoid repeated token layout reads while staying on a symbol. The existing Tower document query, ECS/type metadata, canonical signature formatter, background snapshot preparation and stale-reply guards remain authoritative and unchanged. This is browser interaction code, not a new language analysis model or worker protocol.

Debugging: initial solid-panel selection failed because a capturing window blur listener also received editor focus loss. Checking event.target against the window retains real window dismissal while permitting panel text selection. The initial focused run then passed 18/18 checks. A broader 52-check run passed 51; its sole failure was Playwright clock.pauseAt(new Date()) racing the installed clock, not a hover assertion. Both dwell tests now install a fixed clock and pause one minute later; the final hover rerun passes 18/18 in 24.1 s, including both desktop and mobile profiles. The other 34 completion, delayed-diagnostic and interaction cases passed in the broad run. New tests verify preview hit-test passthrough, pointer following, exact 799/800 ms behavior with continued movement, frozen placement, text selection, 20% margin retention versus 30% dismissal, symbol-switch timer reset, blank-space suppression and timer cancellation. Desktop/mobile screenshots were inspected for both opacity states and viewport placement.

Environment/reproduction: Windows PowerShell, main after initial pull 24f9aa8, Node/Playwright Chromium; verified every asset in the existing Pages a4aa9fa manifest before restoring its unchanged compiler/Wasm/support artifacts with build/hover-dwell-restore.mjs. TOWER_REQUIRE_BACKENDS=1 npm run build --prefix playground succeeds (build/hover-dwell-build.log). node playground/scripts/verify-local.mjs passes all 67 artifact hashes and both desktop/mobile execution, grammar, persistence, native downloads, completion and highlighting checks (build/hover-dwell-local.log). Run npx playwright test tests/browser/hover.spec.mjs from playground for the final focused suite (build/hover-dwell-clock-regression.log); broader results are in build/hover-dwell-regression.log.

Performance: moved the benchmark timestamp to window capture so it starts before the new document-level mouse listener. node playground/scripts/benchmark-hover.mjs http://127.0.0.1:4173/ build/hover-dwell-timing.json measures 20 fresh documents per profile, actual mouse events, DOM insertion and a task after requestAnimationFrame. Cached hover sends zero worker requests. Desktop median DOM/paint boundary: 0.5/2.4 ms, p95 paint boundary 10.6 ms; mobile: 0.5/2.2 ms, p95 8.3 ms. This is browser-observed timing, not monitor latency or a literal zero-time guarantee. No artificial preview delay or per-mousemove semantic request was introduced. No compiler/native runtime code changed; existing published artifacts were validated rather than rebuilt. Publication and live checks follow separately.

## 2026-11-19 — Tower-written C output, shared optimizer control and comment metadata (implementation in progress)

Request: add optional formatted C output, share the optimizer switch with fast interpretation, retain/strip comments, place C then bytecode disassembly after LLVM optimized, and validate C/C++ compiler portability and native performance. User clarified that project logic should be Tower source and dependency/old-compiler compatibility matters more than insisting on strict C89-only facilities.

Research: LLVM's historical C backend was removed in the LLVM 3.1 era (https://releases.llvm.org/3.1/docs/ReleaseNotes.html). JuliaHub's separate LLVM-CBE currently documents LLVM 22 support (https://github.com/JuliaHubOSS/llvm-cbe). This checkout uses a pinned LLVM 20 browser source and LLVM 19 native comparison backend. Chose a direct Tower Foundation-to-C emitter instead of adding another LLVM-coupled native dependency. The existing .tower backend already invokes LLVM's C API and reconstructs compilable Foundation after a scalar O2 pipeline; optimized C reuses that exact path. cpp_name/c_name declaration reading and symbol mangling are already Tower implementations, but they do not infer C++ record/call ABI; C output accepts plain C link names and diagnoses C++ declarations requiring wrappers.

Implementation: compiler/c-emitter.tower and c-runtime.tower produce hosted C from shared Foundation components, using transient naming/storage indexes only. Unoptimized C keeps structured control flow. Optimized C emits the reconstructed Foundation graph, including explicit labels, scalar values and traps. Integer values use unsigned storage, explicit signed views, wrapping arithmetic, range-checked conversions and division guards. Raw memory accesses use memcpy helpers with explicit Tower byte layout and address arithmetic. The output has C89-style declarations/control flow, uses stdint.h when available, and otherwise has a small LP64 / Microsoft-Borland __int64 adapter. Compile-time width assertions and a runtime endian check reject incompatible profiles. The browser profile is 64-bit little endian; CLI target selection can request 32-bit layout. No claim of support for 16-bit pointers, Harvard memory, big endian, arbitrary embedded libc, or an actually tested Borland compiler is made.

Comments are a byte-buffer metadata field on FoundationNode, owned/disposed by Tower. The existing native lexer adapter transports already-classified spans; Tower chooses attachment and canonical block-comment spelling. The common formatter emits this metadata into compilable Foundation. LLVM reconstruction collects comments at module scope, preserving text without inventing an instruction association after optimization. C neutralizes trigraph/backslash-splicing text. The UI adds a persisted preserve-comments checkbox beside the existing O0/O2 LLVM checkbox; this controls instructions, C and fast bytecode. CLI gains --emit c and --strip-comments. Browser C is unchecked by default, has a download footer/highlighting, and follows LLVM optimized immediately before the moved bytecode pane.

Environment: Windows PowerShell/Node; Docker tower_build with /work mounted from C:/Sandbox/tower and tower_host_cache mounted at /cache. Native build /cache/c-native uses /cache/llvm-bc-module-bootstrap/towerc and LLVM 19. Browser build is /work/build/browser-wasi, LLVM/cross cache /cache/llvm-bc-browser, WASI SDK 34 under /cache/wasi. A temporary tower-c-validation container installs GCC/G++ 13 for independent validation. MSVC 14.44 BuildTools is available via vswhere. The first generated factorial/increment C passed Clang 19 -std=c89 -pedantic -Wall -Wextra -Werror and C++98, producing 720 and 721.

Debugging/trials: the first emitter draft used infix expressions in if/call arguments, which the deliberately small Foundation grammar rejects. Lowered these into ordinary named temporaries and formatted using Tower's own formatter; no precedence grammar was added. A native source view is string_view, not string, so the mechanical comment-span bridge needed data() rather than c_str(). CLI output validation needed its Tower driver allowlist updated in addition to the host output transport. Pointer print was corrected during semantic review to Tower's fixed-width hexadecimal address spelling (not string dereferencing). Initial test fixtures incorrectly attempted unequal-width bits; corrected to equal-width bit reinterpretation and explicit convert.

Initial validation: all 278 existing Node/Wasm tests pass with the new frontend. Strict Clang/GCC C89 and C++98 at O0/O2 already pass execution, calls/recursion, structs, memory, inference, templates, collections and all integer operators against graph/native execution. These are interim results, not publication results. Full differential corpus, new metadata/UI tests, MSVC matrix, timing comparisons, sanitizer checks and deployment are still pending; final findings follow below.

Further implementation and debugging: lexer highlights must be captured before frontend_module_session resets its session. The first attachment attempt read the reset session and silently lost all comments; capturing paired spans on the Tower-owned module before reset fixes entry and imported source. Comment round-trip tests then found an extra initial blank line when trailing metadata moved to module scope; the common formatter now indents comment lines and emits an idempotent first item. Warm compiler/module caches before allocation baselines. The frozen semantic reference predates comment attachment, so compare executable semantics after stripping metadata and independently round-trip the complete canonical text. Native formatting assertions correctly rejected interim unformatted Tower files; the Tower formatter resolves them, and failure diagnostics now identify the filename. The browser persistence test's init script was overwriting settings on reload; initialize only once per browser session.

Portability refinements: C89 leaves negative signed division rounding implementation-defined, so the generated helper now divides unsigned magnitudes and explicitly restores quotient/remainder signs. Strings longer than 96 bytes use short-line byte initializers, avoiding C89's small guaranteed literal limit. Comment preprocessing tests cover trigraphs and trailing backslashes; escaped backslash text ends in a non-whitespace character to prevent GCC's permissive whitespace-before-newline splicing. Function ABI signatures preserve int32_t/int64_t, with explicit bit-storage conversions at calls/returns. Primitive and pointer width/alignment assertions supplement the endian check. Ordinary i386 LLVM layouts fail the pre-existing eight-byte i64-alignment contract. A supported wasm32 description plus GCC/Clang -m32 -malign-double, using C99/C++11 integer headers, passes the 32-bit hosted tests; ordinary -m32 and pointer-width mismatches are rejected. This does not add an i386 Tower backend profile.

MSVC /W4 /WX exposed dead fallback returns, unused labels, and an unreachable main return after a proven non-returning call. Simply deleting that last return made GCC C89 -O0 diagnose a missing return; putting it in a comma expression still triggered MSVC C4702. The Tower-owned c-control module derives reachability/returnability directly from Foundation entities, preserves comments from skipped statements, and suppresses dead labels/statements. Optional GCC/Clang/MSVC non-return annotations communicate the proven property; other compilers get plain C and a fallback main return. No warnings are disabled. A first strict matrix passed 304 checks, then 352 after constant-control/long-string/rounding fixtures, then 368 including preprocessing. The final signed ABI corpus and all final publication checks are recorded below. The MSVC runner initializes its toolchain once, builds both C/C++ at /Od and /O2, and executes hidden processes with timeouts. Final native compiler snapshot: /cache/c-native/towerc-c-final, SHA-256 7ad9dd4e74890b82d1804a1faf2e7f26c1d7d8d35bdaf08e4bb54d342bf18da1. Snapshotting prevents a concurrent linker from replacing the executable during a matrix run (an earlier overlapping profile trial failed with PermissionError for that reason).

## 2026-11-19 - Five-pixel hover hold, delayed retargeting and useful documentation

This supersedes the previous percentage-based hover margin at the user's request. The pinned panel now holds within exactly five CSS pixels on each side (and while still over its original source symbol). A different meaningful symbol inside that margin starts an 800 ms retarget dwell while the old content remains visible. Its border darkens from #48656c to #2f4248 to signal the pending change. Movement within the same candidate preserves the timer; changing candidates restarts it; returning to the panel/original symbol or blank margin cancels the pending switch and restores the border. A completed dwell replaces the content with an already-opaque panel anchored at the new symbol. Existing Escape/edit/scroll/compiler-change cancellation also clears this candidate. The initial translucent, click-through, pointer-following preview remains immediate.

Removed generic Syntax labels, entity IDs, component counts and binding IDs from the hover presentation. A bare echoed token has no tooltip; even a meaningful typed entry omits its code heading when that heading would only repeat the token. ## 2026-11-19: pinned compiler worlds and component queries (plan)

Pulled main through 32282ad, preserving the upstream C backend and hover changes.
The next parallel-phase prerequisite is explicit lifetime ownership. The user
confirms the desired compiler world resembles an independent Lua state/V8 isolate
and must support browser live compiler services. Today worker/Wasm isolation is
real, but the native compiler still obtains its store from tower.cpp's singleton.
ModuleEnvironment owns source/module/cache/session state, while component type
registries and native grammar caches still need explicit world migration.

Start with structural views in the existing Tower EntityStore. An open view pins
the store's entities/components and dense per-type query indexes. Coordinators
reject structural mutation during the view, defer zero-reference reclamation,
and reclaim after the last view closes. Refcounts/view state remain coordinator
owned; this does not add atomics or make arbitrary raw payload writes safe.
Workers borrow batches under the scheduler's declared access contracts and return
before the coordinator closes their view. Separate stores remain independent.

Integrate the view into the compiler's layout kernel execution boundary. Discovery
and structural publication remain outside that boundary. Add Tower functional
fixtures for independent stores, nested views, deferred parent/component/type
reclamation, retained entities, structural rejection and stable query batches.
Check interpreter/LLVM/round-trip behavior and real compiler rebuilds; benchmark
the serial cost before claiming a useful parallel prerequisite. No new native
implementation and no completed singleton removal or threaded phase claim.

Implemented EntityView/EntityQuery in the existing Tower entity library and
opened/closed views around semantic layout kernels, including the error path.
Independent stores remain mutable while another is pinned. Last-reference releases
queue an entity once; a retained queued entity survives draining. Reclamation
cannot recursively admit a view while dismantling containment/components. This
uses existing explicit retain/release ownership, not language garbage collection.
The native entity types are opaque, so no owned C/C++ changes were needed.

The first fixture trials used comparisons inside call arguments and an expression
directly in `if`, exceeding current Foundation/Tower syntax. Replaced them with
ordinary locals; no parser changes. Graph interpretation then passed, but optimized
LLVM reconstruction rejected `llvm.ctpop.i32`, produced from the library's bit
idioms. Added scalar population-count reconstruction (integer widths through 64)
using ordinary Foundation arithmetic/bit operations over the same entities.
LLVM's contract counts set bits and returns the input integer type:
[LLVM 20.1 LangRef](https://releases.llvm.org/20.1.0/docs/LangRef.html#llvm-ctpop-intrinsic).
Vector/wider types retain explicit diagnostics.

The dedicated population fixture first used a bit-clearing loop; this pipeline
did not recognize it as ctpop, so the IR assertion correctly failed. Replaced it
with the scalar parallel bit-summing idiom and checked the optimized IR contains
ctpop. Also corrected untyped large literals and narrowed masks before checked
numeric conversion. The fixture now tests every byte value, repeated-byte u32/u64
patterns, zero, full-width values and high bits against an independent reference.
Both widths, graph/fast execution, canonical text, raw/optimized reconstruction
and Wasm output pass. The world fixture covers nested views, query tails, invalid
and cross-world ranges, structural rejection and deferred ownership reclamation.

  `left.tower` at byte 44. Adding only `import right;` to the entry makes the
  unchanged left module compile and print `42\n`, despite left never importing
  right. All three observed outcomes are asserted by the probe.

Root cause: `frontend-compilation.tower` attaches all dependency statements to
`program.root` and passes one collected root list into `semantic_compile`.
`SemanticContext` has shared function/type lookup tables without per-module
visibility. The loader already retains canonical paths, dependency edges and
source entities; preserve these owners through binding rather than inventing
another semantic graph or changing path syntax.

## 2026-11-19 — Inspect grammar roles and compiled replacement trees

The increment example exposed a language-query selection defect: every Bedrock
reader leaf inherited the nearest `SyntaxNode`, and `format_summary` printed that
whole declaration/term/template followed by the generic label `grammar`. Replacement
body inspection walked the balanced declaration-reader tree rather than the already
compiled replacement tree, so function names, address operators and capture holes
could not explain their separate roles.

The query now reads the same SyntaxNode/SyntaxSource/SyntaxPattern/LexerTable layouts
from one type-only Tower module. No layout or semantic representation changes.
Tower snapshots a bounded preview of effective reference alternatives at each
declaration boundary and retains compiled replacement trees plus their source capture
entities. These are disposable indexes of existing entities. Three narrow native
read-only adapters bridge the current Version's still-native lookup maps; classification,
source locations, comments, canonical previews, capture interpretation and function
signature lookup remain Tower code. The JavaScript layer only renders query fields.
Later `=` overrides and `|=` extensions cannot retroactively change earlier reference
hovers. Pending forward dependencies are identified as unresolved at that declaration.

Grammar hovers distinguish rule definition/assignment, alternative separators,
capture bindings, references, literals, exclusion sets and their members, repetition,
lexical patterns, contextual token mode, highlighting metadata and module imports.
Replacement hovers traverse the actual parsed tree and distinguish substitutions,
calls, address/dereference operations, declarations and control flow. A known function
reference uses the ordinary checked function table and shared Foundation signature
formatter. Capture categories are explicitly grammar categories; the query does not
invent concrete runtime types before expansion/substitution. Attached comments are
shown separately from the compact preview. All source ranges remain byte offsets
until the existing UI UTF-8/UTF-16 conversion.

Implementation trials: the first bootstrap compile diagnosed bare Syntax* constants
(Tower constants are zero-argument functions), then aggregate vector_push (by-value
struct parameters are not implemented). Changed those uses to ordinary calls and
reserve/copy ownership transfer respectively. Retained entities are released before
query/session disposal. Shared parser component ABI remains covered by the existing
layout and round-trip tests.

The first executable grammar tests caught a component/payload access mistake:
entity_component_get returns the component handle, so inspection must call
entity_component_data before reading SyntaxNode. Corrected this and reran imports,
grammar, ordinary typed hovers and repeated-query allocation checks successfully.
Additional whole-tree trials exposed two important cases: a replacement shared by
alternatives with Number versus CoreOperand captures, and an unreachable rule whose
template only compiles when a later Statement extension activates it. Capture hover
now reports the ordered union of categories. Shared replacement previews explicitly
identify that their syntax tree comes from the first compiled alternative; they do
not claim one concrete runtime type. Pending templates are filled at their first
activation and then retained without later overrides changing their interpretation.
The role table also covers generated functions, parameters, structs/enums, fields,
binary values, assignment destinations and loop control, using actual parsed nodes.
